Hoddesdon.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of the Lee Valley
s1loc: Hoddesdon sits on the River Lea and the New River in the Borough of Broxbourne, with its marquee draw the Grade I listed Rye House Gatehouse, the brick survivor of a 15th-century fortified manor that gave its name to the Rye House Plot of 1683 against Charles II. The 1835 Clock Tower anchors the High Street, the remains of Rawdon House recall a 17th-century mansion, and Rye House Quay on the Lee Navigation pulls visitors to the waterside.

The leisure and activity layer leans hard on the Lee Valley Regional Park, with the Lee Valley White Water Centre at nearby Waltham Cross built for the London 2012 Olympic canoe slalom and now running rafting, kayaking and paddleboarding all year. Barclay Park and Lowewood give the town centre its green space, while Rye House Stadium, long the home of the Rye House Rockets speedway team, kept the motor-sport crowd coming.

Heritage and culture run through Rawdon House and the medieval origins of the belfry that preceded the Clock Tower, with the Lowewood Museum charting the story of Broxbourne and Hoddesdon and a year-round calendar of markets and events around the High Street. The towpaths of the Lee Navigation and the New River, an early 17th-century engineered watercourse, thread heritage walks through the heart of the town.

The visitor trade rests on day-trippers from across the metropolitan area, with the Lee Valley campsites, riverside moorings and hotel and guest-house base serving the park. Broxbourne and Rye House stations on the West Anglia line bring walkers, anglers and watersports visitors in from London Liverpool Street, and the surrounding Lee Valley draws families to its lakes, marinas and nature reserves through the season.

Wilmslow.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of east Cheshire
s1loc: Wilmslow's marquee draw sits just outside the town at Quarry Bank, the National Trust's vast Industrial Revolution site where Samuel Greg's 18th-century cotton mill still turns its machinery on the power of the River Bollin, with the Apprentice House, workers' cottages and gardens telling the full story. The town's own Victorian streets, St Bartholomew's parish church and the Anglo-Saxon roots of the settlement give the centre its heritage backbone.

The leisure and activity layer runs through The Carrs, a 71-acre riverside park along the Bollin linking the town centre to open Cheshire countryside, and Lindow Common Nature Reserve, a birch-and-heathland Site of Special Scientific Interest with footpaths around Black Lake. Mossways Park and the wider Bollin Valley Way give walkers and cyclists miles of green corridor, with family days out across parks, woodland and the river.

Heritage and culture reach back to Lindow Moss, where the preserved Iron Age bog body known as Lindow Man was discovered in 1984, now in the British Museum. The town keeps a lively events calendar around the Wilmslow Artisan Market, Wizard of the Edge walks toward nearby Alderley Edge, and the galleries and independent venues that have grown up alongside its prosperous Cheshire commuter community.

The visitor trade is anchored by a strong hotel and country-house base across the Alderley Edge and Mottram St Andrew belt, serving golfers, walkers and Manchester Airport business travellers. Wilmslow station on the West Coast Main Line puts the town minutes from the airport and Manchester, and the surrounding Peak District fringe and Cheshire heritage draws make it a year-round day-trip base.

Grays Thurrock.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of Thurrock
s1loc: Grays anchors the Thurrock waterfront on the north bank of the Thames, with the riverside walk passing The Gull, an 1860 lightship moored at Grays Beach, and the Thurrock History Museum and Thameside Theatre housed in the Thameside Complex on Orsett Road. The Art Deco State Cinema on George Street, opened in 1938, remains a local landmark, while the river frontage and the Grays town wharf carry the town's maritime story.

The leisure and activity layer is led by Grays Beach Riverside Park, a sand-and-playground spot beside the Thames, and the 200-acre Chafford Gorges Nature Park with its woodlands, meadows and lakes set in former chalk quarries. Davy Down Riverside Park, the Thurrock Thameside Nature Park and the RSPB Rainham Marshes nearby give families and walkers wetland and estuary trails across the season.

Heritage and culture run to the two Thames forts: Tilbury Fort, where Elizabeth I rallied troops against the Spanish Armada, and the Victorian Coalhouse Fort at East Tilbury, both guarding the estuary. The Thameside Theatre, built in 1971 as the only theatre in Thurrock, programmes drama and music, and the History Museum traces the borough from Roman Mucking to the docks.

The visitor trade is shaped by Lakeside Shopping Centre and its retail park at West Thurrock, among the largest retail destinations in Europe and a huge day-trip draw, alongside a growing hotel base. Grays station on the c2c line links the town directly to London Fenchurch Street and Southend, while the Dartford Crossing and surrounding Thames-side attractions keep visitors flowing through the area year-round.

Upminster.region: Upminster and the London Borough of Havering
Upminster.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of east Havering
s1loc: Upminster's signature landmark is Upminster Windmill, a Grade II* listed smock mill of 1803 restored to become the only working windmill in Greater London, standing beside St Laurence parish church whose tower reaches back to the medieval village. The Upminster Tithe Barn, a scheduled monument dating to around 1450, has long housed a museum of agricultural and domestic nostalgia and frames the town's deep rural heritage.

The leisure and activity layer spreads into Hornchurch Country Park nearby, a 100-acre mosaic of woodland, wetland and meadow on the former RAF Hornchurch airfield, and Stubbers Adventure Centre at North Ockendon, a 130-acre site with three lakes offering sailing, windsurfing, climbing, archery and canoeing. The Ingrebourne Valley and Upminster Park give the town centre its everyday green space for walkers and families.

Heritage and culture run through the Thames Chase Community Forest, whose centre near Upminster keeps a 17th-century heritage barn, orchards and trails, alongside Upminster Hall, a Grade II* timber-framed building now the clubhouse of Upminster Golf Club on Hall Lane. The Cranham and Corbets Tey lanes preserve the old village character, and a steady events calendar runs around the windmill and the parish.

The visitor trade leans on Upminster's position at the eastern edge of the District line and c2c services into London Fenchurch Street, making it a gateway between the capital and the Essex countryside. The local hotel and guest-house base serves day-trippers heading to Thames Chase, Stubbers and the Ingrebourne, while the surrounding Havering green belt and Brentwood-fringe draws keep the season busy.

New Milton.region: New Milton and the New Forest coast
New Milton.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of the New Forest coast
s1loc: New Milton sits on the southern edge of the New Forest National Park, with its marquee draw the Sammy Miller Motorcycle Museum at Bashley, home to around 500 rare and restored machines assembled by trials legend Sammy Miller MBE. The town's distinctive water tower of 1900 stands over the High Street, and Barton-on-Sea, just south, frames the coast with its clifftop walks and views across the Solent to the Isle of Wight.

The leisure and activity layer runs along the coast and into the forest, from the shingle and beach huts of Hordle Cliff and Barton-on-Sea to the quiet, garden-fringed Ballard Lake close to the town centre. Milford-on-Sea and its seafront promenade, the spit walk out to Henry VIII's Hurst Castle, and the woodland borders of the National Park give families beaches, walks and activity across the year.

Heritage and culture take in Hurst Castle, the Tudor artillery fort guarding the Solent with its lighthouse and gun emplacements, and Spinners Garden at Pilley with its national collection of trilliums and woodland of azaleas and magnolias. The Barton-on-Sea Coastguard Cottages, the New Forest heathland heritage and a calendar of community and seafront events round out the town's cultural life.

The visitor trade is built on the New Forest hotel, country-house and guest-house base, with golf, riding and walking holidays drawing visitors through the season. New Milton station, opened in 1888 on the South Western main line, brings travellers from London Waterloo in around two hours, while Bournemouth, Christchurch and the wider forest keep the surrounding area busy with day-trippers and coastal breaks.

Rothwell.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of south Leeds
s1loc: Rothwell sits in the Lower Aire Valley south of Leeds, its heritage anchored by Holy Trinity Church and the long story of Rothwell Colliery, the 'Fanny Pit' that produced coal from 1867 until 1983. The pit head and railway lands have since become Rothwell Country Park, a Yorkshire Wildlife Trust site whose summit gives 360-degree views over Leeds, Bridgewater Place and Temple Newsam across the valley.

The leisure and activity layer centres on Springhead Park, the formal-and-natural town park created between 1935 and 1937 with playgrounds, a skatepark, tennis courts refurbished in a recent investment, crown green bowling, an aviary and a cafe. Rothwell Country Park adds a sculpture trail, pond trail and wildlife paths through a corridor of restored green space linking the town to the River Aire and the wider Aire Valley.

Heritage and culture run through the medieval and Victorian core, with Holy Trinity Church on its historic site, the memory of the coal-mining community preserved in the Country Park sculptures, and the grand Temple Newsam house and estate just to the north with its Tudor-Jacobean mansion, Capability Brown parkland and rare-breeds farm. The town keeps a calendar of community events and gala days through the warmer months.

The visitor trade is shaped by Rothwell's position on the edge of Leeds, with the city's hotel base, the M1 and M62 and Leeds station putting Temple Newsam, the Royal Armouries and the city's attractions within easy reach. The Lower Aire Valley green spaces, the country parks and nearby Castleford and the Xscape leisure complex draw walkers, families and day-trippers across the season.

Formby.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of the Sefton coast
s1loc: Formby's marquee draw is the National Trust's Formby pinewoods and dunes on Victoria Road, one of the few remaining English strongholds of the red squirrel and one of North-West Europe's most important sand-dune systems. The wide beach, the high dunes and the Ravenmeols and Lifeboat Road frontage give the town a sweeping coastline, with rare natterjack toads breeding in the dune slacks and the Irish Sea views drawing visitors year-round.

The leisure and activity layer runs along the Sefton Coastal Path, a 21-mile route from Crosby to Southport that threads Formby Beach, the Ravenmeols Dunes Local Nature Reserve and the Ainsdale National Nature Reserve to the north. Formby Golf Club, a championship links of 1884 set among the maritime pines, and the neighbouring Formby Ladies course make the town a destination for golfers as well as walkers and beach families.

Heritage and culture trace the dunes' past as the old asparagus fields that fed Liverpool, remembered in the National Trust's heritage trails, alongside the prehistoric human and animal footprints exposed on the foreshore. Just south at Crosby Beach, Antony Gormley's Another Place sets 100 cast-iron figures across three kilometres of sand, one of the best-loved public artworks in the country and a major draw on the coast.

The visitor trade leans on day-trippers and coastal-break visitors served by guest houses and the wider hotel base around Southport and the Sefton coast. Formby station on the Merseyrail Northern line links the town directly to Liverpool and Southport, the National Trust car parks fill in season, and the surrounding nature reserves, golf links and Hightown estuary keep the area busy across the year.
